summary: Specifies two authenticated encryption algorithms that are nonce misuse resistant, meaning they do not fail catastrophically if a nonce is accidentally repeated. It is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group.

eli5.summary: Normally using the same one-time number twice ruins a secret code. These codes still stay mostly safe if someone makes that mistake.

questions: how does aes-gcm-siv differ from aes-gcm
subtitle: Authenticated encryption that stays safe even if a nonce is accidentally repeated.

tldr.problem: Standard authenticated encryption algorithms like AES-GCM fail catastrophically if a nonce (one-time number) is used twice with the same key, exposing the encrypted data.
tldr.mechanism: AES-GCM-SIV derives fresh keys for each message using the nonce, and uses two passes to authenticate the plaintext before encryption. If a nonce repeats, only identical plaintexts produce identical ciphertexts, revealing only that equality.
tldr.outcome: The scheme remains secure enough for practical use even when nonces are reused, making it suitable for situations where nonce uniqueness cannot be fully guaranteed.

today: RFC 8452 is an Informational RFC published by the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG). It specifies AES-GCM-SIV for scenarios where nonce misuse resistance is important, such as in multi-encryptor or stateless systems.

sections.title: The Nonce Reuse Problem
sections.content:
Authenticated Encryption with Additional Data (AEAD) protects messages by combining confidentiality (secrecy) and integrity (detecting tampering) in a single operation. The most popular AEAD, AES-GCM, is fast and widely used.

However, AES-GCM and many other AEADs share a critical vulnerability: if the same key and nonce pair is used to encrypt two different messages, both messages are completely exposed. The RFC notes that while specifications require nonce uniqueness, this is difficult to guarantee in practice. For example, when multiple encryptors share a key or when state cannot be reliably maintained, nonce collisions can occur.

This memo specifies AES-GCM-SIV, which degrades gracefully in this scenario. If a nonce repeats, identical plaintexts will produce identical ciphertexts, leaking only the equality—the minimum information a deterministic algorithm must reveal.
sections.eli5: Secret codes usually require using a different number each time. If you mess up and use the same number twice, everything breaks. This new code is designed to break less badly if you make that mistake.

sections.title: Core Design: Two Keys and Two Passes
sections.content:
AES-GCM-SIV uses a two-pass encryption strategy. For each message, it first derives fresh per-nonce keys from the master key, nonce, and a counter. This step is critical: fresh keys for each nonce prevent the birthday-bound limitations that affect standard AES-GCM, allowing far more messages and blocks to be encrypted safely.

The first pass authenticates the plaintext (not the ciphertext) using POLYVAL, a polynomial authenticator similar to GHASH used in AES-GCM. The authentication tag is XORed with the nonce and encrypted to produce the final tag. The second pass encrypts the plaintext using AES in counter mode, with the tag itself serving as the initial counter block.

This design ensures that if a nonce repeats, the derived keys differ (because they depend on the nonce), but identical plaintexts will deterministically produce identical tags and identical ciphertexts. Non-identical plaintexts remain hidden even under nonce reuse.
sections.eli5: The algorithm makes a special number from your password and the one-time number. It then uses that special number to create a code that proves the message is real, and another code to scramble it. If you use the same one-time number again, you get the same scrambled result if the message is the same, but different messages still stay secret.

sections.title: POLYVAL: The Authentication Primitive
sections.content:
POLYVAL is a polynomial authentication tag computed over a binary field, similar to GHASH but with a different construction that better supports nonce-based key derivation. It operates in a 128-bit binary field defined by the irreducible polynomial x^128 + x^127 + x^126 + x^121 + 1.

POLYVAL takes a key and a series of field elements (the padded additional data, padded plaintext, and a length block encoding the bit lengths). It produces a single 128-bit tag by iteratively applying a "dot" operation (multiplication in the field followed by scaling). The RFC documents the exact relationship between POLYVAL and GHASH: POLYVAL is the byte-reversed GHASH applied to byte-reversed inputs, allowing hardware implementations to reuse existing AES-GCM support.
sections.eli5: POLYVAL is the part that checks if a message is real. It mixes a secret number with the message in a special mathematical way to create a proof that only someone who knows the secret could create.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption Process
sections.content:
Encryption takes a 16- or 32-byte master key, a 96-bit nonce, plaintext and additional data of variable length. It outputs a ciphertext 16 bytes longer than the plaintext (the extra 16 bytes are the authentication tag).

The first step derives the message-authentication and message-encryption keys by encrypting blocks containing a 32-bit counter and the nonce. For AES-128, four blocks (counters 0–3) yield 128 bits each of authentication and encryption key; for AES-256, six blocks yield 256 bits of encryption key. The plaintext and additional data are padded to multiples of 16 bytes, and the length block (encoding their bit lengths) is appended. POLYVAL authenticates this padded input, producing a tag that is XORed with the nonce and encrypted to form the final authentication tag. The plaintext is then encrypted in counter mode, starting from the tag with its most significant bit set to one.

Decryption reverses this: it derives keys identically, decrypts the ciphertext in counter mode to recover the plaintext, recomputes the authentication tag over the recovered plaintext, and compares it to the transmitted tag in constant time. Critically, the plaintext is not released until authentication succeeds, preventing the release of forged data.
sections.eli5: To send a secret message, the code makes two special numbers from your password and one-time number. One special number is used to create a proof of the message, and the other scrambles it. To read the message, the receiver does the same steps and checks the proof before trusting the message.

sections.title: Security Properties and Nonce Handling
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that AES-GCM-SIV does not intend to enable nonce reuse as a policy. Rather, it provides the best possible security in the event of accidental reuse. The nonce misuse-resistant property guarantees only that identical plaintexts produce identical ciphertexts under reuse; they do not prevent information leakage from repeated nonces.

For this reason, the RFC recommends using randomly generated nonces. When nonces are random, the probability of even a single repeat across billions of messages is negligible (remaining negligible up to 2^102 nonces for a 96-bit nonce). The RFC provides usage bounds for various scenarios. With 256 or fewer repeats of any single nonce, AES-GCM-SIV can securely encrypt up to 2^29 messages of 1 GiB each, or 2^61 messages of 16 KiB each. With truly random nonces, up to 2^64 messages of 128 KiB each can be encrypted.

A critical implementation requirement: plaintext must never be released before authentication is verified. Large plaintexts could tempt implementations to stream decryption before checking the tag, introducing a system vulnerability. Fresh key derivation per nonce also prevents a known attack where an attacker could zero the POLYVAL key by controlling the master key.
sections.eli5: The code is designed to be forgiving if you mess up one-time numbers, but it still relies on the message itself staying secret even if the same one-time number is used twice. The safest way to use it is still to make sure one-time numbers are random and never repeat if possible.
